title: Phytoremediation
wikitext:
{{Short description|Decontamination technique using living plants}}
[[File:Phytoextraction diagram.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|Some heavy metals such as copper and zinc are removed from the soil by moving up into the plant roots.]]
{{Pollution sidebar|Soil}}

'''Phytoremediation'''  technologies use living [[plants]] to clean up soil, air and water contaminated with [[pollutant]]s.<ref>{{cite book|author=R. K. Sinha, D. Valani, S. Sinha|title= Microremediation, Phytoremediation, and Vermiremediation Biotechnologies for Contaminated Lands and Soil|publisher=Nova Science Publishers|location=Hauppauge, NY|year=2010}}</ref><ref name=Reichenauer2008>{{cite journal |vauthors=Reichenauer TG, Germida JJ |title=Phytoremediation of organic contaminants in soil and groundwater |journal=ChemSusChem |volume=1 |issue=8–9 |pages=708–17 |year=2008 |pmid=18698569 |doi=10.1002/cssc.200800125 |bibcode=2008ChSCh...1..708R }}</ref>  The term is an amalgam of the Greek ''phyto'' (plant) and Latin ''remedium'' (restoring balance).  It is a type of [[bioremediation]].

Phytoremediation is proposed as a sustainable alternative to conventional remediation methods,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Islam |first=Merajul |date=2024-04-20 |title=Phytoremediation as a green and sustainable prospective method for heavy metal contamination: a review |url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2024/su/d3su00440f |journal=RSC Sustainability |volume=2 |issue=5 |pages=1269–1288 |doi=10.1039/D3SU00440F |doi-access=free }}</ref> although it has never been used at large scales.{{needcite|date=June 2026}} Other forms of bioremediation, such as those employing [[microorganism]]s,  have so far been more successful.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Franzius |first1=Volker |last2=Grimsky |first2=Detlef |last3=Möhlenbruch |first3=Norbert |last4=Dworshak |first4=Ulf |title=Ullmann's Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry |chapter=Soil, 4. Remediation of Soil and Land |date=2011 |doi=10.1002/14356007.o24_o03 |isbn=978-3-527-30385-4 }}</ref>

== Processes ==
[[File:Mechanisms involved in phytoremediation.png|thumb|upright=1.8| {{center|Mechanisms involved in [[hydrocarbon]] phytoremediation<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Rohrbacher | first1=Fanny | last2=St-Arnaud | first2=Marc | title=Root Exudation: The Ecological Driver of Hydrocarbon Rhizoremediation | journal=Agronomy | publisher=MDPI AG | volume=6 | issue=1 | date=2016-03-09 | issn=2073-4395 | doi=10.3390/agronomy6010019 | page=19| doi-access=free | bibcode=2016Agron...6...19R }}</ref>}}]]
Major phytoremediation mechanisms include '''phytoextraction, phytostabilization, phytovolatilization, and phytofiltration.'''<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Priya |first1=A. K. |last2=Muruganandam |first2=Muthiah |last3=Ali |first3=Sameh S. |last4=Kornaros |first4=Michael |date=2023-05-02 |title=Clean-Up of Heavy Metals from Contaminated Soil by Phytoremediation: A Multidisciplinary and Eco-Friendly Approach |journal=Toxics |volume=11 |issue=5 |page=422 |doi=10.3390/toxics11050422  |doi-access=free|issn=2305-6304 |pmc=10221411 |pmid=37235237 |bibcode=2023Toxic..11..422P }}</ref>

=== Phytoextraction ===
{{See also|Hyperaccumulator#Phytoremediation}}
Phytoextraction (or ''phytoaccumulation'' or ''phytosequestration'') aims to exploit the ability of some plants to absorb certain contaminants from soil or water.  In principle, the roots take up substances from the soil or water and concentrate them above ground in the plant biomass.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Ali|first1=Hazrat|last2=Khan|first2=Ezzat|last3=Sajad|first3=Muhammad Anwar|title=Phytoremediation of heavy metals—Concepts and applications|journal=Chemosphere|volume=91|issue=7|pages=869–881|doi=10.1016/j.chemosphere.2013.01.075|pmid=23466085|year=2013|bibcode=2013Chmsp..91..869A}}</ref> 

Organisms that can uptake high amounts of particular metal-containing compounds are called [[hyperaccumulators]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rascio|first1=Nicoletta|last2=Navari-Izzo|first2=Flavia|title=Heavy metal hyperaccumulating plants: How and why do they do it? And what makes them so interesting?|journal=Plant Science|volume=180|issue=2|pages=169–181|doi=10.1016/j.plantsci.2010.08.016|pmid=21421358|year=2011|bibcode=2011PlnSc.180..169R |s2cid=207387747 }}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Pilon-Smits|first=Elizabeth|date=2005-04-29|title=Phytoremediation|journal=Annual Review of Plant Biology|volume=56|issue=1|pages=15–39|doi=10.1146/annurev.arplant.56.032604.144214|pmid=15862088|bibcode=2005AnRPB..56...15P |issn=1543-5008}}</ref> Since arsenic (As) is a toxic industrial by-product, As-accumulating plants -e.g. [[Chinese brake]] - have been proposed to concentrate and then remove As from contaminated soils.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tu |first1=Cong |last2=Ma |first2=Lena Q. |last3=Bondada |first3=Bhaskar |title=Arsenic Accumulation in the Hyperaccumulator Chinese Brake and Its Utilization Potential for Phytoremediation |journal=Journal of Environmental Quality |date=2002 |volume=31 |issue=5 |pages=1671–1675 |doi=10.2134/jeq2002.1671 |pmid=12371185 }}</ref>

Phytoextraction could also be performed by non-hyperaccumulating plants (e.g. [[Populus]] and [[Salix]]).  Although they take up only low levels of pollutants, owing to their high growth rate, such plants could in principle remove a considerable amount of contaminants from the soil.<ref>Guidi Nissim W., Palm E., Mancuso S., Azzarello E. (2018) "Trace element phytoextraction from contaminated soil: a case study under Mediterranean climate". Environmental Science and Pollution Research https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-018-1197-x</ref> 
<!--
Of course many pollutants kill plants, so phytoremediation is not a panacea. For example, chromium is toxic to most higher plants at concentrations above 100 μM·kg−1 dry weight.<ref name=toxicCr>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.envint.2005.02.003|title=Chromium toxicity in plants|year=2005|last1=Shanker|first1=A.|last2=Cervantes|first2=C.|last3= Lozatavera|first3=H.|last4=Avudainayagam|first4=S.|journal=Environment International|volume=31|issue=5|pages=739–753|pmid=15878200|bibcode=2005EnInt..31..739S }}</ref>-->

Hyperaccumulating plants are often [[metallophyte]]s, i.e. they hyperaccumulate metals.  Metallophytes are the basis of [[phytomining]], a proposed technology for collecting valuable metals without excavating.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Morse |first1=Ian |title=Down on the Farm That Harvests Metal From Plants |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/02/26/science/metal-plants-farm.html |access-date=27 February 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=26 February 2020}}</ref>

One challenge to phytoremediation is that heavy metals are often insufficiently mobile to be taken up by the plants, hyperaccumulators or otherwise.  This challenge prompted the invention of assisted phytoextraction, whereby a  [[chelator]] is added to soil to increase metal solubility or mobilization so that the plants can absorb them more easily.  A typical chelator is [[edta]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Doumett|first1=S.|last2=Lamperi|first2= L.|last3=Checchini|first3=L.|last4=Azzarello|first4=E.|last5=Mugnai|first5=S.|last6=Mancuso|first6=S.|last7=Petruzzelli|first7=G.|last8=Del Bubba|first8=M.|date=August 2008|title=Heavy metal distribution between contaminated soil and ''Paulownia tomentosa'', in a pilot-scale assisted phytoremediation study: Influence of different complexing agents|journal=Chemosphere|volume=72|issue=10|pages=1481–1490|doi=10.1016/j.chemosphere.2008.04.083|pmid=18558420|bibcode=2008Chmsp..72.1481D|hdl=2158/318589|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref name=Salt1998>{{cite journal |vauthors=Salt DE, Smith RD, Raskin I |title=Phytoremediation |journal=Annual Review of Plant Physiology and Plant Molecular Biology |volume=49 |pages=643–668 |year=1998 |pmid=15012249 |doi=10.1146/annurev.arplant.49.1.643 |s2cid=241195507 }}</ref>

=== Phytostabilization ===
Phytostabilization lowers the mobility of substances in the soil, for example, by limiting the [[Leaching (pedology)|leaching]] of substances from the [[soil]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Lone|first1=Mohammad Iqbal|last2=He|first2=Zhen-li|last3=Stoffella|first3=Peter J.|last4=Yang|first4=Xiao-e|date=2008-03-01|title=Phytoremediation of heavy metal polluted soils and water: Progresses and perspectives|journal=Journal of Zhejiang University Science B|volume=9|issue=3|pages=210–220|doi=10.1631/jzus.B0710633|pmid=18357623|issn=1673-1581|pmc=2266886}}</ref> It focuses on the long term stabilization and containment of the pollutant. Unlike phytoextraction, phytostabilization focuses mainly on sequestering pollutants in soil near the roots but not in plant tissues. Pollutants become less bioavailable. Stabilization results in reduced erosion, runoff, leaching, in addition to reducing the bioavailability of the contaminant.<ref name=":3" /> 

Phytostabilization involving a vegetative cap has been used to stabilize and contain [[mine tailings]].<ref>{{Citation|journal=Environ Health Perspect |year=2008 |volume=116 |issue=3 |pages=278–83 |title=Phytostabilization of Mine Tailings in Arid and Semiarid Environments—An Emerging Remediation Technology |vauthors=Mendez MO, Maier RM |url=http://www.ehponline.org/members/2007/10608/10608.html |doi=10.1289/ehp.10608 |pmid=18335091 |pmc=2265025 |bibcode=2008EnvHP.116..278M |postscript=. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081024115430/http://www.ehponline.org/members/2007/10608/10608.html |archive-date=2008-10-24 }}</ref> Some [[soil amendment]]s decrease radiosource mobility – while at some concentrations the same amendments will ''increase'' mobility.<ref name="Fesenko-Howard-2012">{{cite book | editor1-last=Fesenko | editor1-first=Sergey | editor2-first=Brenda J. | editor2-last=Howard | title=Guidelines for Remediation Strategies to Reduce the Radiological Consequences of Environmental Contamination | publisher=[[International Atomic Energy Agency]] | publication-place=Vienna | year=2012 | isbn=978-92-0-134110-5}}</ref><ref name="Fesenko-et-al-2016">{{cite book | editor1-first=Dharmendra K. | editor1-last=Gupta | editor2-first=Clemens | editor2-last=Walther | last1=Fesenko | first1=Sergey | last2=Howard | first2=Brenda J. | last3=Sanzharova | first3=Natalya | last4=Vidal | first4=Miquel | title=Impact of Cesium on Plants and the Environment | chapter=Remediation of Areas Contaminated by Caesium: Basic Mechanisms Behind Remedial Options and Experience in Application | publisher=Springer International Publishing | publication-place=Cham | date=2016-10-15 | isbn=978-3-319-41524-6 | doi=10.1007/978-3-319-41525-3_15 | pages=265–310}}</ref>  [[Root mat]]s of [[meadow grass]]es are possibly effective at demobilising radiosource materials especially with certain combinations of other agricultural practices.<ref name="Fesenko-Howard-2012" /><ref name="Fesenko-et-al-2016" /> The particular grasses are proposed makes a significant difference.<ref name="Fesenko-Howard-2012" /><ref name="Fesenko-et-al-2016" />

=== Phytodegradation ===
[[File:Phytoremediation by Degradation.svg|thumb|The roots secrete enzymes that degrade (breakdown) organic pollutants in the soil.]]

Phytodegradation (also called phytotransformation) is the use of plants to degrade organic pollutants.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=http://www.unep.or.jp/Ietc/Publications/Freshwater/FMS2/2.asp|title=Phytoremediation Processes|website=www.unep.or.jp|access-date=2018-03-28|archive-date=2019-01-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190102092030/http://www.unep.or.jp/Ietc/Publications/Freshwater/FMS2/2.asp}}</ref> This process has been proposed to deal with herbicides, [[trichloroethylene]], and [[Methyl tert-butyl ether|methyl ''tert''-butyl ether]].<ref name=":3" /> 

Phytotransformation, which is closely related to phytodegradation, is defined as the chemical modification of substances by plants, ideally with beneficial effects.<ref name=Kvesitadze>{{Citation |author=Kvesitadze, G. |title=Biochemical Mechanisms of Detoxification in Higher Plants |publisher=Springer |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |year=2006 |isbn=978-3-540-28996-8 |display-authors=etal |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/biochemicalmecha00kves_0 }}</ref>  The term "Green Liver" has been used to describe phytotransformation,<ref>{{Citation |first=H. |last=Sanderman |title=Higher plant metabolism of xenobiotics: the "green liver" concept |journal=Pharmacogenetics |volume=4 |issue=5 |pages=225–241 |year=1994 |doi=10.1097/00008571-199410000-00001|pmid=7894495 }}.</ref> as plants can be thought to behave analogously to the human [[liver]] when dealing with these [[xenobiotic]] compounds (foreign compound/pollutant).<ref>{{Citation |author=Burken, J.G. |chapter=2. Uptake and Metabolism of Organic Compounds: Green-Liver Model |editor1=McCutcheon, S.C. |editor2=Schnoor, J.L. |title=Phytoremediation: Transformation and Control of Contaminants |publisher=John Wiley |location=Hoboken, NJ |year=2004 |doi=10.1002/047127304X.ch2 |chapter-url=http://www3.interscience.wiley.com/cgi-bin/summary/106569012/SUMMARY?CRETRY=1&SRETRY=0 |series=A Wiley-Interscience Series of Texts and Monographs |isbn=978-0-471-39435-8 |pages=59–84 }}{{Dead link|date=February 2021 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ramel | first1 = F. | last2 = Sulmon | first2 = C. | last3 = Serra | first3 = A.A. | last4 = Gouesbet | first4 = G. | last5 = Couée | first5 = I. | year = 2012 | title = Xenobiotic sensing and signalling in higher plants | journal = Journal of Experimental Botany | volume = 63 | issue = 11| pages = 3999–4014 | doi = 10.1093/jxb/ers102 | pmid = 22493519 | doi-access =  }}</ref> 

[[Trinitrotoluene]] phytotransformation has been extensively researched and a transformation pathway has been proposed.<ref name="Subra">{{Citation |first1=Murali |last1=Subramanian |first2=David J. |last2=Oliver |name-list-style=amp |first3=Jacqueline V. |last3=Shanks |title=TNT Phytotransformation Pathway Characteristics in Arabidopsis: Role of Aromatic Hydroxylamines |journal=Biotechnol. Prog. |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=208–216 |year=2006 |doi=10.1021/bp050241g |pmid=16454512 |bibcode=2006BioPr..22..208S |s2cid=28085176 }}.</ref>

=== Phytostimulation ===
Phytostimulation (or rhizodegradation) is the enhancement of [[soil life|soil microbial]] activity for the degradation of organic contaminants, typically by organisms that associate with [[root]]s.<ref name=":4" /> This process occurs within the [[rhizosphere]], which is the layer of soil that surrounds the roots.<ref name=":4" /> Plants release carbohydrates and acids that stimulate microorganism activity which results in the biodegradation of the organic contaminants.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Dzantor|first=E. Kudjo|date=2007-03-01|title=Phytoremediation: the state of rhizosphere 'engineering' for accelerated rhizodegradation of xenobiotic contaminants|journal=Journal of Chemical Technology & Biotechnology|volume=82|issue=3|pages=228–232|doi=10.1002/jctb.1662|bibcode=2007JCTB...82..228D |issn=1097-4660}}</ref> In the ideal case, the microorganisms detoxify pollutants.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bhatnagar |first1=Sonal |last2=Kumari |first2=Reeta |date=2013 |title=Bioremediation: A Sustainable Tool for Environmental Management – A Review |journal=Annual Review & Research in Biology |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=974–993}}</ref> 

[[Leaf litter]] and organic matter from plants can stabilize [[Soil biology|microbial soil biosiversity]] and minimize further loss of microogranisms from contaminants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stefanowicz |first1=Anna M. |last2=Kapusta |first2=Paweł |last3=Zubek |first3=Szymon |last4=Stanek |first4=Małgorzata |last5=Woch |first5=Marcin W. |date=2020 |title=Soil organic matter prevails over heavy metal pollution and vegetation as a factor shaping soil microbial communities at historical Zn–Pb mining sites |journal=Chemosphere |volume=240 |article-number=124922 |doi=10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.124922 |pmid=31563718 |bibcode=2020Chmsp.24024922S |issn=0045-6535 |url=https://ruj.uj.edu.pl/xmlui/handle/item/87434 }}</ref> Phytostimulation has been tested with petroleum, PCBs, and PAHs.<ref name=":3" /> Phytostimulation might also be applicable to [[atrazine]] degradation by [[hornwort]].<ref>{{Citation|last1=Rupassara|first1=S. I.|title=Degradation of Atrazine by Hornwort in Aquatic Systems|year=2002|last2=Larson|last3=Sims|last4=Marley|first2=R. A.|first3=G. K.|first4=K. A.|s2cid=97080119|journal=Bioremediation Journal|volume=6|issue=3|pages=217–224|doi=10.1080/10889860290777576|bibcode=2002BiorJ...6..217R |name-list-style=amp}}.</ref>

=== Phytovolatilization ===
[[File:Phytoremediation by Phytovolatilization.svg|thumb|Contaminates are then broken down and the fragments are then subsequently transformed and volatilized into the atmosphere.]]

Phytovolatilization is the removal of substances from soil or water with release into the air, as a result of phytotransformation to more volatile and/or less polluting substances.<ref name=":4" /> Additionally, contaminants can be volatilized from the root zone.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Limmer|first1=Matt|last2=Burken|first2=Joel|date=2016-07-05|title=Phytovolatilization of Organic Contaminants|journal=Environmental Science & Technology|volume=50|issue=13|pages=6632–6643|doi=10.1021/acs.est.5b04113|pmid=27249664|issn=0013-936X|bibcode=2016EnST...50.6632L|doi-access=free}}</ref> Evidence has been presented that selenium (Se) and mercury (Hg) can removed from soil through phytovolatilization.<ref name=":2"/>  Selenium is volatilized as [[dimethyl selenide]] and mercury as the element.<ref name=Salt1998/> Poplar trees have been touted for removing VOCs, exploiting the high rate of transpiration for this tree species.<ref name=":3" />

=== Rhizofiltration ===
[[Rhizofiltration]] is a process that filters water through a mass of roots to remove toxic substances or excess [[nutrients]]. The pollutants remain absorbed in or adsorbed to the roots.<ref name=":4" /> This process is often used to clean up contaminated groundwater through planting directly in the contaminated site or through removing the contaminated water and providing it to these plants in an off-site location.<ref name=":4" /> In either case though, typically plants are first grown in a greenhouse under precise conditions.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Surriya|first1=Orooj|last2=Saleem|first2=Sayeda Sarah|last3=Waqar|first3=Kinza|last4=Kazi|first4=Alvina Gul|pages=1–36|doi=10.1016/b978-0-12-799937-1.00001-2|title = Soil Remediation and Plants|year = 2015|isbn = 978-0-12-799937-1|s2cid=126742216 }}</ref>

=== Biological hydraulic containment ===
Biological [[hydraulic containment]] occurs when some plants, like poplars, draw water upwards through the soil into the roots and out through the plant, which decreases the movement of soluble contaminants downwards, deeper into the site and into the groundwater.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Phytotechnology and Photosynthesis|last1=Evans|first1=Gareth M.|last2=Furlong|first2=Judith C.|date=2010-01-01|publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Ltd|isbn=978-0-470-97515-2|pages=145–174|doi=10.1002/9780470975152.ch7}}</ref>

=== Phytodesalination ===
Phytodesalination uses halophytes (plants adapted to saline soil) to extract salt from the soil to improve its fertility.<ref name=":0" />

== Role of genetics ==
Breeding programs and [[genetic engineering]] are powerful methods for enhancing natural phytoremediation capabilities, or for introducing new capabilities into plants.  Genes for phytoremediation may originate from a [[micro-organism]] or may be transferred from one plant to another variety better adapted to the environmental conditions at the cleanup site. For example, genes encoding a nitroreductase from a bacterium were inserted into tobacco and showed faster removal of TNT and enhanced resistance to the toxic effects of TNT.<ref name="Hannink">{{Citation |last1=Hannink |first1=N. |last2=Rosser |first2=S. J. |last3=French |first3=C. E. |last4=Basran |first4=A. |last5=Murray |first5=J. A. |last6=Nicklin |first6=S. |last7=Bruce |first7=N. C. |s2cid=6965013 |title=Phytodetoxification of TNT by transgenic plants expressing a bacterial nitroreductase |journal=Nature Biotechnology |year=2001 |volume=19 |issue=12 |pages=1168–72 |doi=10.1038/nbt1201-1168 |pmid=11731787 }}.</ref>
Researchers have also discovered a mechanism in plants that allows them to grow even when the pollution concentration in the soil is lethal for non-treated plants. Some natural, biodegradable compounds, such as exogenous [[polyamine]]s, allow plants to tolerate higher concentrations of pollutants and increase pollutant uptake.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gill |first1=Sarvajeet Singh |last2=Tuteja |first2=Narendra |date=2010-12-01 |title=Reactive oxygen species and antioxidant machinery in abiotic stress tolerance in crop plants |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0981942810001798 |journal=Plant Physiology and Biochemistry |volume=48 |issue=12 |pages=909–930 |doi=10.1016/j.plaphy.2010.08.016 |pmid=20870416 |bibcode=2010PlPB...48..909G |issn=0981-9428|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Hyperaccumulators and biotic interactions ==
{{Main|Hyperaccumulator}}

A plant is said to be a [[hyperaccumulator]] if it can concentrate the pollutants in a minimum percentage which varies according to the pollutant involved (for example: more than 1000 mg/kg of dry weight for [[nickel]], [[copper]], [[cobalt]], [[chromium]] or [[lead]]; or more than 10,000 mg/kg for [[zinc]] or [[manganese]]).<ref name="BB89">{{Citation |first1=A. J. M. |last1=Baker |first2=R. R. |last2=Brooks |title=Terrestrial higher plants which hyperaccumulate metallic elements – A review of their distribution, ecology and phytochemistry |journal=Biorecovery |year=1989 |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=81–126 }}.</ref>  This capacity for accumulation is due to '''hypertolerance''', or ''phytotolerance'': the result of adaptative evolution from the plants to hostile environments through many generations. A number of interactions may be affected by metal hyperaccumulation, including protection, interferences with neighbour plants of different species, mutualism (including [[mycorrhiza]]e, [[pollen]] and seed dispersal), commensalism, and [[biofilm]].<ref name="Biotechnology Advances 2011 pp. 645–653">{{cite journal | title=Hyperaccumulators, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and stress of heavy metals | journal=Biotechnology Advances | volume=29 | issue=6 | date=2011-11-01 | issn=0734-9750 | doi=10.1016/j.biotechadv.2011.04.006 | pages=645–653 | url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0734975011000474 | access-date=2021-12-09| last1=Miransari | first1=Mohammad | pmid=21557996 | url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Pavlova De La Fuente SÁNchez-Mata Rufo pp. 671–681">{{cite journal | last1=Pavlova | first1=D. | last2=De La Fuente | first2=V. | last3=SÁNchez-Mata | first3=D. | last4=Rufo | first4=L. | title=Pollen morphology and localization of Ni in some Ni-hyperaccumulator taxa of Alyssum L. (Brassicaceae) | journal=Plant Biosystems | publisher=Informa UK Limited | volume=150 | issue=4 | date=2014-12-12 | issn=1126-3504 | doi=10.1080/11263504.2014.989284 | pages=671–681| s2cid=84954143 }}</ref><ref name="Visioli DEgidio Sanangelantoni 2021 p.">{{cite journal | last1=Visioli | first1=Giovanna | last2=D'Egidio | first2=Sara | last3=Sanangelantoni | first3=Anna M. | title=The bacterial rhizobiome of hyperaccumulators: future perspectives based on omics analysis and advanced microscopy | journal=Frontiers in Plant Science | volume=5 | date=2021-06-02 | pmid=25709609 | doi=10.3389/fpls.2014.00752 | page=752| pmc=4285865 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

Plant growth-promoting bacteria, or PGPB, are soil bacteria in the rhizosphere that enhance plant productivity by increasing nutrient bioavailability, secreting metabolites and hormones that stimulate increased plant growth, and secreting antibiotics that prevent pathogenic infection.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Emmanuel |first1=Obianuju Chiamaka |last2=Babalola |first2=Olubukola Oluranti |date=2020-10-01 |title=Productivity and quality of horticultural crops through co-inoculation of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and plant growth promoting bacteria |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0944501320304377 |journal=Microbiological Research |volume=239 |article-number=126569 |doi=10.1016/j.micres.2020.126569 |pmid=32771873 |bibcode=2020MbRes.23926569E |issn=0944-5013|url-access=subscription }}</ref> PGPB have been shown to assist heavily with enhancing the transport of soil pollutants like [[heavy metals]] from the soil into the roots of hyperaccumulators via phytostimulation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Poria |first1=Vikram |last2=Dębiec-Andrzejewska |first2=Klaudia |last3=Fiodor |first3=Angelika |last4=Lyzohub |first4=Marharyta |last5=Ajijah |first5=Nur |last6=Singh |first6=Surender |last7=Pranaw |first7=Kumar |date=2022-10-21 |title=Plant Growth-Promoting Bacteria (PGPB) integrated phytotechnology: A sustainable approach for remediation of marginal lands |journal=Frontiers in Plant Science |language=English |volume=13 |article-number=999866 |doi=10.3389/fpls.2022.999866 extract:
Phytoremediation  technologies use living plants to clean up soil, air and water contaminated with pollutants.  The term is an amalgam of the Greek phyto (plant) and Latin remedium (restoring balance).  It is a type of bioremediation.
Phytoremediation is proposed as a sustainable alternative to conventional remediation methods, although it has never been used at large scales. Other forms of bioremediation, such as those employing microorganisms,  have so far been more successful.
